title: Multi-head latent attention (MLA)
summary: How DeepSeek's MLA caches one 512-wide latent plus a 64-wide RoPE key per token, absorbs the up-projections so decode never rebuilds keys, and what that means for kernels and serving.
outcomes: Compute KV cache per token for MHA, GQA, MQA and MLA from a model config
Explain how low-rank joint compression lets each head rebuild keys and values from one latent
Show why absorbing W_UK and W_UV is exact and why it makes MLA decode MQA-shaped
Explain why RoPE breaks absorption and how a shared decoupled RoPE key fixes it
Choose absorbed vs plain attention and the right parallelism when serving MLA models

lessons.title: Why per-head keys and values make the KV cache huge

blocks.md:
Recall from the GPU course: during decoding, every past token's key and value vectors stay in GPU memory (the **KV cache**) so the next token can attend to them without recomputing them. Decoding is memory-bound, so the size of this cache decides how many requests fit in a batch and how long a context can get.

In standard **multi-head attention (MHA)**, each of the $n_h$ heads has its own key and its own value of size $d_h$, in every one of the $l$ layers. The DeepSeek-V2 paper writes the cache per token as:

blocks.tex: \text{MHA cache per token} = 2\, n_h\, d_h\, l \ \text{elements}
blocks.caption: The 2 counts keys and values. Elements, not bytes: multiply by 2 for BF16.

blocks.md:
Plug in the attention shape of DeepSeek-V3 ($n_h = 128$ heads, $d_h = 128$, $l = 61$ layers) as if it used plain MHA: $2 \times 128 \times 128 \times 61 = 1{,}998{,}848$ elements, about 4.0 MB per token in BF16. A single 128K-token context (131,072 tokens) would need about 524 GB of cache, for one sequence.

The cache is big because every head stores its own key and value. Cut the number of stored heads and the cache shrinks.

Two earlier fixes do exactly that:

- **Multi-query attention (MQA)**, Shazeer 2019: all query heads share one key head and one value head. Cache: $2 d_h l$.
- **Grouped-query attention (GQA)**, Ainslie et al. 2023: query heads are split into $n_g$ groups, each sharing one key and value head. Cache: $2 n_g d_h l$.

Both save memory by giving many heads the *same* keys and values, and both cost quality. In DeepSeek-V2's ablation (Appendix D.1, 7B dense models, 1.33T tokens), MMLU was 45.2 with MHA, 41.2 with GQA (8 groups) and 37.9 with MQA.

blocks.title: KV cache for one sequence vs context length (V3 attention shape)

scenes.caption: With 128 heads of size 128 and 61 layers in BF16, MHA needs about 524 GB at 131,072 tokens. Note the log scale: each gridline is 10x.
GQA with 8 groups stores 8 key and value heads instead of 128, a 16x cut (32.7 GB at 128K). MQA stores one, a 128x cut (4.1 GB).
MLA, as configured in DeepSeek-V3, caches 576 elements per token per layer: 9.2 GB at 128K. That sits between MQA and GQA-8, while every head still gets its own keys and values.
Batch 8 sequences: everything scales linearly. Simplified: real servers also store weights and activations, and page the cache in blocks.

blocks.title: Cached elements per token per layer

scenes.caption: Per layer, MHA caches $2 \times 128 \times 128 = 32{,}768$ numbers for every token. This dwarfs everything else.
Same numbers as KiB per token over all 61 layers in BF16: 3904, 244, 68.6 and 30.5 KiB. MLA is 1.76% of MHA, a 56.9x reduction.

blocks.prompt: MLA in DeepSeek-V2 and V3 caches $d_c + d_h^R = 512 + 64 = 576$ elements per token per layer, with $d_h = 128$. A GQA model with how many groups would cache the same amount?
blocks.reveal: GQA caches $2 n_g d_h = 256\, n_g$ per layer, so $n_g = 576 / 256 = 2.25$. The DeepSeek-V2 paper states exactly this: with $d_c = 4 d_h$ and $d_h^R = d_h / 2$, the MLA cache equals GQA with only 2.25 groups (Table 1). The surprise is the quality claim that comes with it: the paper reports MLA performing better than MHA, not just better than GQA.

blocks.md: The paper counts cache size in **elements**, regardless of storage precision. Quantizing the cache to FP8 or lower is a separate, stackable trick. When comparing headline numbers, check whether both sides use the same precision.

Cache size per token is set by what you store per token per layer. MQA and GQA shrink it by sharing keys and values across heads. MLA's bet is different: store one small learned vector per token and let each head derive its own keys and values from it.

blocks.question: A model with 128 query heads switches from MHA to GQA with 8 groups, keeping $d_h$ and layer count fixed. By how much does its KV cache shrink?
options: 8x, because there are 8 groups
2x, because keys and values are both still stored
16x, because 128 key and value heads become 8
128x, because only one head is stored
blocks.explain: Cache is $2 n_g d_h l$ for GQA vs $2 n_h d_h l$ for MHA, so the ratio is $n_h / n_g = 128 / 8 = 16$. MQA would be the 128x case.

blocks.question: Why didn't DeepSeek simply use MQA, which has an even smaller cache than MLA?
options: MQA cannot be used with a KV cache
In their 7B ablation MQA lost clearly to MHA on hard benchmarks, and they wanted MHA-level quality
MQA needs more GPU memory for weights
MQA does not support causal masking
blocks.explain: DeepSeek-V2 Appendix D.1 shows MQA at 37.9 MMLU vs 45.2 for MHA at 7B. MLA was designed to get a small cache without paying that quality cost.

lessons.title: Low-rank joint compression: cache one latent, rebuild every head

blocks.md:
MLA (multi-head latent attention, introduced in DeepSeek-V2) keeps full multi-head attention, with $n_h$ distinct keys and values per token, but changes how they are produced. Instead of projecting the layer input $h_t$ straight to keys and values, it first squeezes $h_t$ into a short **latent vector** $c_t^{KV}$ of size $d_c$, and then expands that latent into every head's key and value.

"Joint" means one latent feeds both keys and values. "Low-rank" means the expansion goes through a $d_c$-dimensional bottleneck, so all $2 n_h d_h$ key and value numbers of a token are determined by just $d_c$ numbers.

blocks.tex: c_t^{KV} = W^{DKV} h_t, \qquad k_t^{C} = W^{UK} c_t^{KV}, \qquad v_t^{C} = W^{UV} c_t^{KV}
blocks.caption: Eqs. 9 to 11 of DeepSeek-V2. D means down-projection, U means up-projection. Only the latent is cached; the per-head keys and values can always be rebuilt from it.

blocks.md:
A tiny example. Hidden size $d = 4$, two heads with $d_h = 2$, latent size $d_c = 2$, and no position encoding yet. The learned matrices are:

- $W^{DKV}$ has rows $(0.5, 0, 0.5, 0)$ and $(0, 0.5, 0, -0.5)$.
- $W^{UK}$: head 1 is the identity; head 2 has rows $(1, 1)$ and $(1, -1)$.
- $W^{UV}$: head 1 has rows $(1, -1)$ and $(0, 1)$; head 2 is $2I$.

Three tokens arrive with $h_1 = (1, 0, 2, -1)$, $h_2 = (0, 1, 1, 1)$ and $h_3 = (2, 1, 0, 0)$. Their latents are $c_1 = (1.5, 0.5)$, $c_2 = (0.5, 0)$ and $c_3 = (1, 0.5)$.

blocks.title: What each scheme writes to the cache (toy layer)

scenes.caption: Token 1. MHA stores head 1 key (1.5, 0.5), head 2 key (2, 1), then the two values (1, 0.5) and (3, 1): 8 numbers. MLA stores only the latent (1.5, 0.5).
Token 2 adds 8 more numbers to the MHA cache and 2 to the MLA cache.
After three tokens: 24 numbers vs 6. The ratio is $2 n_h d_h / d_c = 8 / 2 = 4$ and it holds at any length.
Nothing is lost: head 2's key for token 1 is $W^{UK}_2 c_1 = (1.5 + 0.5,\ 1.5 - 0.5) = (2, 1)$, exactly what MHA stored. Every cached MHA number is a fixed linear function of the latent.

blocks.md: The catch is the bottleneck. In MHA the keys and values of all heads can be any $2 n_h d_h$ numbers. In MLA they must lie in a $d_c$-dimensional subspace, because they are all linear in $c_t^{KV}$. In DeepSeek-V2 and V3 that is 32,768 numbers per layer generated from 512 ($d_c = 512$, $n_h = 128$, $d_h = 128$). Training learns $W^{DKV}$, $W^{UK}$ and $W^{UV}$ together so the latent keeps what attention needs.

blocks.title: One MLA layer in DeepSeek-V3, with sizes

scenes.caption: Keys and values: the 7168-wide input is projected down to a 512-wide latent, then up to 128 heads of keys and 128 heads of values.
Position: a separate 64-wide key carries rotary position (RoPE). It is one vector shared by all heads. Lesson 4 explains why it must be separate.
Queries are also squeezed through a 1536-wide latent. This saves activation memory in training; it does not affect the KV cache, since queries are never cached.
What is cached per token per layer: c_KV (512) and k_R (64), 576 numbers. Plain MHA with this shape would cache 32,768.
Decoding one token: compute its c_KV and k_R, append them to the cache, then attend over all cached latents.

blocks.md: Two details from the paper matter in practice. First, DeepSeek-V2 adds RMSNorm layers after the compressed latents and extra scaling factors at these width bottlenecks to keep training stable; in the released V3 code, the cached latent is the RMS-normalized one. Second, DeepSeek-V2-Lite drops the query compression entirely, which shows it is an optional training-memory saving, not part of the cache trick.

MLA is not a compression applied to an already trained model's cache, like PCA on stored keys. The down- and up-projections are ordinary weights learned from scratch during pretraining. Converting an existing MHA or GQA model to MLA needs extra fine-tuning work (see lesson 5).

blocks.question: In DeepSeek-V3, which tensors does an MLA layer write to the KV cache for each new token?
options: The per-head keys $k^C$ and values $v^C$
The query latent $c^Q$ and the key latent $c^{KV}$
The layer input $h_t$, since everything can be recomputed from it
The key-value latent $c^{KV}$ and the shared RoPE key $k^R$
blocks.explain: Only $c^{KV}$ (512) and $k^R$ (64) are cached. Queries are never cached. Caching $h_t$ (7168 wide) would be larger and would force recomputing projections for every past token.

blocks.question: A team doubles $n_h$ from 128 to 256 in an MLA model, keeping $d_c = 512$, $d_h^R = 64$ and the layer count fixed. What happens to the KV cache per token?
options: It doubles, like it would in MHA
It stays the same: the cache holds the latent and shared RoPE key, whose sizes do not depend on $n_h$
It halves, because each head gets a smaller share
It grows by 64 elements per layer for each new head
blocks.explain: MLA cache is $(d_c + d_h^R)\, l$. The number of heads only changes the size of the up-projection weights $W^{UK}$ and $W^{UV}$, not what is stored per token.

lessons.title: Absorbing the up-projections: attend in latent space

blocks.md:
Caching only the latent raises an obvious worry. To compute attention you need each head's keys and values, so a naive decoder would rebuild $k^C_j = W^{UK} c_j$ and $v^C_j = W^{UV} c_j$ for every cached token $j$ at every step.

That is expensive. With DeepSeek-V3's shapes and 4,096 cached tokens, rebuilding keys and values costs $4096 \times 128 \times (128 + 128) \times 512 \approx 68.7$ billion multiply-adds per layer per generated token. The attention itself would only be about 168 million.
The fix uses associativity of matrix products. For head $i$, the score between query $q_{t,i}$ and past token $j$ is a dot product, and the up-projection can move to the query side:

blocks.tex: q_{t,i}^{\top} k^C_{j,i} = q_{t,i}^{\top}\left(W^{UK}_i c_j\right) = \left(W^{UK\top}_i q_{t,i}\right)^{\top} c_j
blocks.caption: Compute the absorbed query once per head per step, then dot it directly with each cached latent. No key is ever materialized.

blocks.tex: o_{t,i} = \sum_j a_{t,j,i}\, W^{UV}_i c_j = W^{UV}_i \Big(\sum_j a_{t,j,i}\, c_j\Big)
blocks.caption: Values work the same way: mix the latents with the attention weights first, then up-project once. W_UV can be folded into the output projection W_O.

blocks.title: Naive vs absorbed scores for toy head 2
blocks.code:
import numpy as np
# toy head 2: d_h = 2, d_c = 2, three cached latents
c = np.array([[1.5, 0.5], [0.5, 0.0], [1.0, 0.5]])
W_UK = np.array([[1.0, 1.0], [1.0, -1.0]])
W_UV = np.array([[2.0, 0.0], [0.0, 2.0]])
q = np.array([1.0, 0.5])
# naive: rebuild every cached key, then dot
k = c @ W_UK.T
s_naive = k @ q
# absorbed: move W_UK onto the query once
q_lat = W_UK.T @ q
s_abs = c @ q_lat
a = np.exp(s_abs / np.sqrt(2))
a = a / a.sum()
# values: mix the latents, then up-project once
c_mix = a @ c
o = W_UV @ c_mix

scenes.caption: The cache holds three 2-wide latents from lesson 2. Head 2 has its own $W^{UK}$ and $W^{UV}$, and the new query is (1, 0.5).
Naive path: rebuild a key for every cached token. Cost grows with cache length times the size of $W^{UK}$.
Naive scores are dot products of q with each rebuilt key.
Absorbed path: multiply the query by the transposed up-projection once, giving a query that lives in latent space.
Dot the latent-space query with the cached latents directly. The scores are identical to the naive ones.
Softmax with scale $1/\sqrt{2}$ (here $d_h = 2$). Token 1 gets the most weight.
Mix the latents with the weights, then up-project once. The result (2.3779, 0.8456) matches the naive weighted sum of rebuilt values exactly.
scenes.output: o = [2.3779, 0.8456]  (naive sum of a_j * v_j gives the same)

blocks.prompt: After absorption, each head's score is a dot product over the 512-wide latent (plus the 64-wide RoPE part) instead of a 192-wide key. Does decoding one token now do more or less arithmetic than the naive rebuild-then-attend path?
blocks.reveal:
**Less overall, though more per score.** Each score now costs 576 multiply-adds instead of 192, so the attention core itself grows from about 168 million to about 570 million multiply-adds per layer at 4,096 cached tokens. But the 68.7 billion multiply-adds of rebuilding keys and values disappear, replaced by two small per-step projections of about 8.4 million each. Total: about 587 million vs about 68.9 billion, roughly 117x less.

Simplified: counts only the attention part of one layer for one new token with DeepSeek-V3 shapes.

blocks.md:
Now look at what the absorbed computation reads. All 128 heads score against the **same** cached vectors $[c_j; k^R_j]$ (576 wide) and mix the **same** $c_j$ as values (512 wide). That is structurally multi-query attention: many query heads, one shared key and value stream. vLLM's MLA code says it plainly: the decode path "simulates" multi-head attention while the compute is like MQA, with key head dimension $d_c + d_h^R$ and value head dimension $d_c$. DeepSeek's FlashMLA write-up notes the same thing: in MLA, K and V are the same data.

So MLA gets MQA-like memory traffic during decoding while each head still sees different keys and values, because each head looks at the latent through its own absorbed query.

blocks.code:
# DeepSeek-V3 inference/model.py, attn_impl == "absorb" (lightly trimmed)
wkv_b = wkv_b.view(n_local_heads, -1, kv_lora_rank)          # per-head [W_UK; W_UV]
q_nope = torch.einsum("bshd,hdc->bshc", q_nope, wkv_b[:, :qk_nope_head_dim])  # absorb W_UK
kv_cache[:bsz, start_pos:end_pos] = kv_norm(kv)                # cache the latent
pe_cache[:bsz, start_pos:end_pos] = k_pe.squeeze(2)            # cache the shared RoPE key
scores = (torch.einsum("bshc,btc->bsht", q_nope, kv_cache[:bsz, :end_pos]) +
          torch.einsum("bshr,btr->bsht", q_pe, pe_cache[:bsz, :end_pos])) * softmax_scale
scores = scores.softmax(dim=-1, dtype=torch.float32)
x = torch.einsum("bsht,btc->bshc", scores, kv_cache[:bsz, :end_pos])  # mix latents
x = torch.einsum("bshc,hdc->bshd", x, wkv_b[:, -v_head_dim:])          # then W_UV
x = wo(x.flatten(2))
blocks.caption: The reference decoder caches kv_cache (512 per token) and pe_cache (64 per token). The naive mode in the same file instead caches full per-head k (192) and v (128).

blocks.md: Absorption is just regrouping a product of matrices: $q^{\top}(W c) = (W^{\top} q)^{\top} c$. It turns MLA decoding into MQA-shaped work over the latent cache, so no per-head key or value is ever stored or rebuilt.

blocks.question: In the toy, the absorbed query for head 2 is (1.5, 0.5). What is head 2's raw score against token 3, whose latent is $c_3 = (1, 0.5)$?
blocks.explain: $1.5 \times 1 + 0.5 \times 0.5 = 1.75$, the same as $q \cdot k_3$ with the rebuilt key $k_3 = (1.5, 0.5)$: $1 \times 1.5 + 0.5 \times 0.5 = 1.75$.

blocks.question: Which property of matrix multiplication makes absorbing $W^{UK}$ into the query legal?
options: Commutativity: $AB = BA$
Associativity: $(AB)C = A(BC)$, so the up-projection can be grouped with the query instead of the latent
Distributivity over the softmax
Invertibility of $W^{UK}$
blocks.explain: Only regrouping is needed. Matrix products are not commutative in general, and $W^{UK}$ is not square (it maps 512 to 128 x 128), so it is not invertible. Lesson 4 shows how RoPE breaks this regrouping.

lessons.title: Decoupled RoPE: why position breaks absorption

blocks.md: DeepSeek models use **RoPE** (rotary position embedding, Su et al.). RoPE splits a query or key into pairs of dimensions and rotates each pair by an angle proportional to the token's position. Write $R_m$ for the rotation at position $m$. Because rotations compose, the score between a rotated query and a rotated key depends only on the relative offset:

blocks.tex: (R_t\, q)^{\top}(R_j\, k) = q^{\top} R_t^{\top} R_j\, k = q^{\top} R_{j-t}\, k

blocks.title: RoPE scores depend only on the offset

scenes.caption: One 2-dimensional pair, $q = k = (1, 0)$, angle 0.5 radians per position, causal mask. Each score is $\cos(0.5\,(t - j))$.
Every cell at offset 1 scores 0.88, wherever the pair sits in the sequence. Position enters only through $t - j$.
Offset 3 scores 0.07 and offset 4 scores -0.42. The rotation between query and key changes with the offset, which is the problem for MLA.

blocks.md: Now apply RoPE to MLA's keys the obvious way, rotating $k^C_j = W^{UK} c_j$. The score for head $i$ becomes:

blocks.tex: \left(R_t\, q^C_{t,i}\right)^{\top} R_j W^{UK}_i c_j = q^{C\top}_{t,i}\; R_{j-t}\, W^{UK}_i\; c_j
blocks.caption: The rotation sits between the query and W_UK, and it is different for every cached position j. There is no single matrix to fold into the query.

blocks.md:
The DeepSeek-V2 paper puts it this way: a RoPE matrix tied to the current token would lie between $W^Q$ and $W^{UK}$, and matrix multiplication is not commutative, so $W^{UK}$ can no longer be absorbed. Decoding would have to recompute the rotated keys of all prefix tokens at every step, which is exactly the cost lesson 3 removed.

The fix, **decoupled RoPE**, splits each head's query and key into two parts. The *content* part ($q^C$, $k^C$, 128 dims per head) gets no rotation, so absorption still works. A separate *position* part carries RoPE: a per-head query $q^R_{t,i}$ and one key $k^R_t$ **shared by all heads**, each $d_h^R = 64$ wide.

blocks.tex: q_{t,i} = [\,q^C_{t,i};\ q^R_{t,i}\,],\quad k_{t,i} = [\,k^C_{t,i};\ k^R_t\,],\quad k^R_t = \mathrm{RoPE}(W^{KR} h_t)
blocks.caption: Eqs. 14 to 17 of DeepSeek-V2. The score is the content dot product plus the position dot product, scaled by 1 over the square root of (d_h + d_h^R) = 192.

blocks.md:
The shared $k^R_t$ must be cached, because it depends on position and cannot be rebuilt from the latent. That is where the cache formula $(d_c + d_h^R)\, l$ comes from: 512 + 64 = 576 elements per token per layer. In the absorbed decoder, the content score uses the latent-space query against $c_j$ and the position score uses $q^R_{t,i}$ against the cached $k^R_j$, the two einsums you saw in lesson 3's code.

One more consequence: when DeepSeek-V2 extended its context from 4K to 128K tokens with YaRN (a method that rescales RoPE frequencies so a model handles longer contexts), it applied YaRN only to the decoupled key $k^R_t$, since that is the only part carrying RoPE.

blocks.title: Cache per token per layer under different RoPE choices

scenes.caption: Latent alone (512) is smallest but has no position information in the keys.
MLA's choice: one shared 64-wide RoPE key adds only 64 elements, for 576 total.
If each of the 128 heads had its own 64-wide RoPE key, the cache would be $512 + 128 \times 64 = 8704$, 15.1x larger. Sharing $k^R$ across heads is what keeps MLA small.
For scale, plain MHA with 128 heads of 128 caches 32,768.

blocks.md: Read the config: in DeepSeek-V3's `config.json`, `kv_lora_rank` is $d_c$ = 512, `qk_rope_head_dim` is $d_h^R$ = 64, `qk_nope_head_dim` is the content part of each head (128) and `v_head_dim` is 128. The query latent `q_lora_rank` is 1536.

blocks.question: A colleague's absorbed MLA decoder applies RoPE at position t to the full 512-wide absorbed query, then dots it with the cached latents. What goes wrong?
options: Nothing, RoPE commutes with the latent projection
It only fails for contexts longer than 4K
The rotation now acts in latent space, which does not equal rotating each head's keys; position information is wrong and the scores no longer match the trained model
The cache size doubles
blocks.explain: RoPE in MLA must only touch the decoupled 64-wide parts. The content part was trained without rotation, and a rotation applied in the 512-wide latent space is not the per-head offset rotation $R_{j-t}$ of the key, so the scores no longer match the trained model.

blocks.question: Why is the decoupled RoPE key $k^R_t$ shared across all heads, while the RoPE query $q^R_{t,i}$ is per head?
options: Keys must be cached and queries do not; sharing the key keeps the cache at $d_c + d_h^R$ instead of $d_c + n_h d_h^R$
Because RoPE only works with a single head
To save FLOPs on the query side
Because the latent already contains position
blocks.explain: Queries are computed for the current token only and discarded, so per-head queries cost no cache. A per-head key would add $n_h d_h^R = 8192$ elements per token per layer in DeepSeek-V3.

lessons.title: MLA in production: kernels, prefill, parallelism, results

blocks.md: What did MLA buy in practice? DeepSeek-V2 Appendix D.2 trained matched MoE models with MHA and with MLA. The small pair (about 16B total parameters, 1.33T tokens) cached 110.6K vs 15.6K elements per token. The large pair (about 250B total, 420B tokens) cached 860.2K vs 34.6K, about 4%. On the four hard benchmarks reported, MLA scored higher than MHA in 7 of 8 comparisons, for example MMLU 59.0 vs 57.5 at the large scale.

blocks.title: DeepSeek-V2 Table 9: MHA vs MLA at two scales

scenes.caption: KV cache per token, thousands of elements. Small: 110.6K vs 15.6K, about 14%. Large: 860.2K vs 34.6K, about 4%. Dividing the MLA numbers by 576 suggests about 27 and 60 layers.
MMLU (5-shot) for the same models: 48.7 vs 50.0 and 57.5 vs 59.0. The smaller cache did not cost quality in these runs.

blocks.md: Do not credit MLA with every DeepSeek-V2 headline. Against DeepSeek 67B, V2 reports a 93.3% smaller KV cache and 5.76x maximum generation throughput (over 50K tokens per second on one 8-GPU H800 node), but the deployed system also used FP8 weights, KV cache quantization to about 6 bits per element, and a sparse MoE. The 42.5% training cost saving comes from MoE, not MLA.

**Decode kernels.** Lesson 3 showed absorbed MLA is MQA-shaped: every query head reads the same cached rows. DeepSeek's FlashMLA write-up (April 2025) estimates the ratio of FLOPs to bytes read for decode attention as about $h_q s_q (d_k + d_v)/d_k$, where $h_q$ is the number of query heads, $s_q$ the query tokens per request (1 without speculative decoding), $d_k = 576$ and $d_v = 512$. With all 128 heads on one GPU this lands near the GPU's ridge point, so they optimized the kernel as compute-bound, unusual for decode attention.

blocks.tex: \text{intensity} \approx \frac{2\, h_q s_q s_k (d_k + d_v)}{2\, s_k d_k} = h_q s_q \cdot \frac{576 + 512}{576} \approx 1.89\, h_q s_q
blocks.caption: FLOPs over bytes (BF16) when s_k cached tokens dominate. Plain MHA reads separate K and V per head, so its intensity stays near s_q.

blocks.title: Decode attention: FLOPs per byte vs heads sharing the cache

x.label: query heads x query tokens (h_q s_q)

scenes.caption: Ridge 258 FLOPs per byte: FlashMLA's figure of about 865 TFLOPS (throttled H800) over 3.35 TB/s. Below the ridge a kernel is memory-bound; above it, compute-bound.

Absorbed MLA grows with the number of heads sharing the latent rows. At 128 heads it reaches about 242, just under the 258 ridge; FlashMLA rounds the ratio to 2 h_q s_q = 256 and treats it as compute-bound. Simplified: ignores query and output bytes.
Split the 128 heads 8 ways with tensor parallelism and each GPU sees 16 heads: about 30 FLOPs per byte, deep in memory-bound territory, and every GPU must still read the whole latent cache.

blocks.md: **Prefill uses the other form.** Absorption trades fewer bytes for more FLOPs per score (576-wide instead of 192-wide). During prefill, many query tokens attend at once and compute is the bottleneck, so vLLM's MLA implementation uses a "compute friendly" path for prefill: it up-projects the latents into ordinary per-head keys and values and runs standard multi-head attention. For decode it uses the "data-movement friendly" absorbed MQA path. For long contexts, prefill up-projects the cached context in chunks so the temporary keys and values fit in a fixed workspace.

**Tensor parallelism duplicates the cache.** In GQA, splitting KV heads across GPUs also splits the cache. MLA has effectively one KV head, so splitting the 128 query heads across GPUs gives every GPU a full copy of the latent cache. vLLM's docs state that DeepSeek-R1 with MLA on a single node at tensor parallel size 8 duplicates the KV cache 8x, and offer decode context parallelism (sharding the cache along the token dimension) to remove it. DeepSeek's own FlashMLA write-up says their decoding instances do not use tensor parallelism for attention, so each GPU keeps all 128 heads.

**Adoption.** DeepSeek-V3 kept V2's MLA dimensions (512, 1536, 64, 128 heads), and other open models ship the same layout; Moonshot's Kimi K2 config, for instance, uses `kv_lora_rank` 512 with 64 heads. For models already trained with MHA or GQA, [MHA2MLA](https://arxiv.org/abs/2502.14837) converts them with partial RoPE removal and an SVD-based low-rank initialization, then fine-tunes on a small fraction (0.6% to 1%) of the pretraining tokens. On Llama2-7B, MHA2MLA alone cuts the KV cache by 68.75% to 87.5%; its headline 92.19% cut also stacks 4-bit cache quantization on top, with about a 1% LongBench drop.

MLA moves the cost of attention from memory to compute: one 576-wide row per token per layer, read by every head. That is a big win for decode, where memory traffic dominates, as long as you keep many heads on the GPU that holds the cache and use the non-absorbed form when compute dominates.

blocks.question: You serve an MLA model on 8 GPUs and KV cache memory is the limit on batch size. Moving attention from 8-way tensor parallelism to 8-way data parallelism (each GPU holds all heads, different requests) mainly helps because:
options: Data parallelism makes the latent smaller
Under tensor parallelism each GPU keeps a full copy of every request's latent cache, so 8 GPUs hold 8 copies; under data parallelism each request's cache lives on one GPU
Tensor parallelism cannot run MLA at all
Data parallelism removes the need for the RoPE key
blocks.explain: The latent is shared by all heads, so splitting heads does not split the cache. vLLM documents this 8x duplication for DeepSeek-R1 at TP 8 and offers decode context parallelism as another way to avoid it.

blocks.question: For a long prompt's prefill, why does vLLM up-project the latents into full keys and values instead of using the absorbed path?
options: The absorbed path gives different numerical results
Prefill does not use a KV cache
Prefill is compute-bound, and the absorbed path does more FLOPs per score (576-wide vs 192-wide dot products), while its memory savings matter little there
RoPE cannot be applied during prefill
blocks.explain: Both paths compute the same function. The absorbed form wins when reading the cache dominates (decode); the plain multi-head form wins when arithmetic dominates (prefill).

blocks.question: A blog says MLA alone cut DeepSeek-V2's KV cache by 93.3% vs MHA. What is wrong with that claim?
options: 93.3% is measured against DeepSeek 67B (a GQA model) for the deployed system, which also quantizes the cache; MLA vs MHA in matched models was 14% to 4% of the MHA cache
Nothing, that is exactly what the paper measured
MLA increases the KV cache
93.3% refers to training cost
blocks.explain: The abstract compares V2 to DeepSeek 67B. The matched MHA vs MLA comparison is Table 9: 15.6K vs 110.6K and 34.6K vs 860.2K elements per token.
